overview: Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

items.text: By 1650, Mwaant Yaav Naweej had connected his capital with Atlantic trade. This commerce included enslaved people as well as forest products.
Lunda outposts participated in copper exchange, while settlements near Lake Mweru linked the interior with eastern commercial routes.
Rulers commissioned artists from client peoples, including Chokwe carvers, to make prestigious court objects.
Accounts of Chibinda Ilunga describe a founding culture hero. They are traditions of legitimacy, not a dated eyewitness biography.
In related Chokwe court art, a chief holds a lamellophone associated with historical recitation and praise. The object shows how music and political knowledge could meet.
